tldr: RoboBuilder introduces a benchmark where AI agents co-design physical robot mechanisms and control programs using standard parts and custom 3D-printed components. When real-world runs fail, agents watch videos of the failures, adjust their simulator and robot designs, and successfully navigate the obstacles.
hero_caption: Overview of RoboBuilder. On the left, an agent co-designs robot mechanisms and control by combining standard parts with custom 3D-printed pieces. On the right, robots that pass in simulation are physically assembled and tested. When a robot fails in the real world, the agent analyzes video footage of the run to autonomously tune physical simulator parameters and redesign the robot for another attempt.
overview:
Autonomous agents powered by LLMs have shown impressive results in code generation and CAD modeling. But can they co-design robots—both hardware and software simultaneously—that physically work in the real world? Designing robots purely in simulation inevitably runs into the Sim-to-Real gap: real-world low friction, loose joints, or slipping gears. In fact, under public nominal part data, none of the 15 initial designs that passed in simulation could cross the physical course.

To address this, the research team developed RoboBuilder, the first agentic robot co-design benchmark that brings physical real-world validation directly into the loop. Agents combine 132 types of block-compatible parts, motors, and custom 3D-printed parts to build robots and control programs that tackle 10 obstacle courses across three difficulty levels. Remarkably, the agent learns the physical parameters of the simulator itself beforehand using requested measurements and real run videos.

Furthermore, every design that passed in simulation was physically assembled by researchers by hand and tested on real courses (135 physical robots in total, taking an estimated 240 hours). When a physical robot failed, researchers fed video of the failure back to the agent. The agent analyzed what broke, corrected both the simulator's physical constants and the robot's design, and closed the "hardware loop" for another try.

Experiments showed that frontier agents (such as Opus 5.5 and GPT-6) invented flexible mechanisms (whegs, cable cars, legged walkers, etc.) that conventional evolutionary search could not reach, crossing 98% of level-1 obstacles. In addition, providing real-world failure videos resolved 72% of level-1 and level-2 failures, boosting real-world success rates up to 93%.
contributions: Built RoboBuilder, the first physical robot co-design benchmark for agents with real-world assembly, physical run testing, and video feedback in the loop.
Established RoboBuilder-Sim and RoboBuilder-Loop, where agents learn and correct physics engine discrepancies from real measurements and run videos.
Demonstrated that four frontier coding agents can autonomously invent and optimize novel mechanisms that conventional black-box search methods cannot produce.
Released a large-scale dataset featuring 135 physically assembled robots (approx. 240 hours), 16,427 simulations, and 461 paired real-to-simulation comparison videos.

sections.heading: Can AI Agents Build Machines That Work in the Real World?
sections.summary: The 'build, test, fix' iterative loop that excels in software development has been expanded to physical robot mechanism design. Because simulation alone cannot prevent slipping tires or disengaging gears, this new benchmark feeds real-world test videos directly back to the agent.
sections.details:
The essence of engineering design lies in the loop of prototyping, testing, learning from failures, and improving. Coding agents have mastered this loop in software because tests take only seconds and results are clear-cut. For physical machines, however, the real test is physical assembly, and simulators harbor countless inaccuracies that only reveal themselves through physical experiments.

Here is the key issue: using a simulator built only on public nominal specs of parts, none of the initial 15 robots that passed in simulation crossed the real course (failing in all 44 physical trials). Tires slipped more than expected, snap-fit joints popped off under weight, gears slipped out of mesh, and weight balance collapsed on slopes. Traditional Sim-to-Real methods calibrate models of a 'fixed robot morphology' using real data, but co-design changes the robot's shape drastically with every iteration. This demands physical models that generalize across entirely unseen designs.

To solve this, the authors propose RoboBuilder. Agents co-design robots and open-loop control programs to cross 10 obstacle courses using block-compatible inventory parts, motors, and up to four copies of one custom 3D-printed part. Furthermore, the agent itself learns the simulator from real run videos and measurements, and when physical runs fail, it inspects the video to redesign both the machine and the simulator. Frontier agents cleared 98% of level-1 tasks and invented whegs (wheel-legs), cable cars, and walking mechanisms that conventional search-based baselines could not find.

captions.F2: Twelve representative robots out of the 135 designed by agents and physically hand-assembled. Highly diverse mechanisms were autonomously devised to match each obstacle: wheg (wheel-leg) mechanisms, giant 3D-printed hoop wheels, cam-driven propulsion systems, rope-crossing gondolas, and spoked wheels that scale walls.

sections.heading: From CAD Generation to Real-World Feedback Loops
sections.summary: While LLM-assisted design and evolutionary robot morphology have been actively studied, most remain confined to simulators. RoboBuilder is the first benchmark to feed physical run results and failure videos back into both design and simulation.
sections.details:
Prior work broadly falls into four categories, but each has missed a critical piece.

### Engineering Design with LLM Agents
A growing body of work uses LLMs to generate CAD scripts or assemble machines in physics sandboxes (such as BesiegeField or BuildArena). However, these treat the simulator as ground truth and have no mechanism to feed real-world physical assembly or test results back into the design.

### Computational Robot Co-Design
Evolutionary and reinforcement learning methods that optimize morphology and control together have a long history. However, most explore parameters within human-defined, rigid design representations (like graph grammars or voxel grids) inside fixed simulators. RoboBuilder agents have no such rigid template; they can construct arbitrary machines using stock inventory parts and free-form CAD code.

### Sim-to-Real and Simulator Learning
To bridge the gap between simulation and reality, researchers have used domain randomization, system identification, and model adaptation from real run data. Recent studies use vision-language models (VLMs) to align physics parameters from video, but they all focus on a specific, fixed robot. There has been no precedent for having an agent learn a generalizable simulator capable of handling unbuilt, novel robots in a co-design setting where morphology changes constantly.

### Agents and Search Systems
Coding agents use tools, reflect on failures, and accumulate skills. Yet while software tests take seconds, assembling and testing physical robots takes hours. This puts a premium on an agent's ability to select every single iteration wisely.

sections.heading: How RoboBuilder Works: Tasks, Physics Learning, Physical Tests, and Loops
sections.summary: RoboBuilder consists of four components: a co-design benchmark (Bench), a learned physics simulator (Sim), physical assembly testing (Lab), and a redesign loop driven by failure videos (Loop). In this framework, the agent refines both the simulator and mechanisms using video observations.
sections.details:
The RoboBuilder system mirrors a practicing engineer's workflow through four core components:

### RoboBuilder-Bench: Defining the Co-Design Benchmark
Given course specifications, the agent must output a robot design $d$ and a motor control program $u$ that crosses the finish line within a time limit and stays upright for 5 seconds. Available materials include 132 part types from an inventory of roughly 3,000 blocks, electronics (up to 4 motors, a battery pack, an IR receiver), and one custom 3D-printed part designed by the agent via CadQuery (Python script, instantiable up to 4 times). There are 10 obstacle types (slopes, walls, steps, crevices, suspension bridges, ropes, continuous bumps, seesaws, inclined U-turns, etc.) across difficulty levels 1 to 3.

### RoboBuilder-Sim: Learning the Simulator
MuJoCo serves as the physics engine, but rigid-body physics engines struggle to capture the flex and detachment tendencies of small block assemblies. Before running the benchmark, the authors had an agent (Opus 5.5) calibrate the simulator. The agent requested bench tests from human operators—such as the tilt angle where sliding begins or the weight at which block joints separate—and entered real measurements. It also compared time-synced physical run videos with simulation, introducing empirical models for stud joint separation, gear tooth skipping, and battery voltage sag. This drastically improved simulation fidelity.

### RoboBuilder-Lab: Physical Assembly and Testing
Designs passing simulation were hand-assembled by researchers following automatically generated assembly guides. Building 135 physical robots took an estimated 240 hours. Real-world physical effects like friction, structural flex, backlash, and center-of-mass shifts cannot be faked.

### RoboBuilder-Loop: Self-Correction from Failure Videos
When a physical run fails, the real run video and the simulated run video are returned to the agent. The agent analyzes behavioral discrepancies between the two, fine-tunes simulator physics parameters if needed, searches for a more robust design, and resubmits.

captions.F3: The co-design task setup and hardware loop workflow. Left: available stock parts and the 10 obstacle courses. Right: the cycle where, following a physical failure after passing simulation, the agent inspects run video, updates physics constants like friction, redesigns a new mechanism, and successfully clears the physical obstacle.

sections.heading: Experimental Results: Agent Invention, the Integration Wall, and the Hardware Loop
sections.summary: Evaluating four frontier agents showed they cleared 98% of level-1 tasks and autonomously invented whegs and specialized hoop wheels. While they struggled with an all-in-one challenge requiring a single robot to clear all courses, closing the loop with real failure videos boosted the real-world pass rate from 73% to 93%.
sections.details:
Evaluated models included Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 in Claude Code, alongside GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol in Codex. Random sampling over the full inventory and genetic algorithms (GA) served as baselines.

### Overwhelming Problem-Solving and Invention by Agents
Agents crossed 98% of level-1 obstacles, 70% at level 2, and 48% at level 3. In contrast, search baselines searching over all parts could not solve a single task (even with 10x compute, GA maxed out at 20% on level 1). Search baselines repeatedly generated flat carts or crawler tracks and could not conceive task-specific mechanisms like climbing arms or rope clamps. Agents created distinctly different structures tailored to each obstacle from scratch (Figure F4).

### The Challenge of 'All-in-One' System Integration
While agents excelled at individual obstacles, they managed at most 60% (6 courses cleared) on the All-in-one challenge, where a single robot must cross all 10 obstacles. Reconciling conflicting requirements into a single design—such as high ground clearance for bumps, narrow track width for bridges, and suspended structures for ropes—proved to be a major bottleneck.

### Real Failure Modes and the Impact of the Hardware Loop
Across all levels, 66% of designs that passed simulation succeeded on the physical course (77% at level 1, 68% at level 2, and 42% at level 3). Primary failure causes were getting stuck on steps/edges (50%), falling off the course (17%), and tipping over (17%) (Figure F6).

Running RoboBuilder-Loop—showing failure videos to the agent for redesign—resolved 13 out of 18 failures (72%) across levels 1 and 2, raising the physical pass rate from 73% to 93% (Figure F7). Seeing tires slip on a ledge from the video, the agent revised its friction parameters, boldly transitioned from wheels to whegs or cam-driven walking legs, and conquered the real course.

captions.F4: t-SNE visualization map of all simulated designs. Robot morphological representations (DINOv2 features) cluster clearly by obstacle type (color-coded) rather than by agent type. This shows agents naturally converge on optimal mechanical structures governed by each task's physical requirements.
captions.F6: Primary physical failure modes for robots that passed simulation: (a) stuck on an edge/step (50%), (b) fall off the track (17%), (c) trapped under the rope (17%), and (d) tip over / roll over (17%). These stem from physical factors like reduced friction and joint flex.
captions.F7: Examples of physical failures overcome via the hardware loop. (a) Initial design failing in reality by getting stuck or falling, (b) redesign in simulation guided by failure video feedback, and (c) the rebuilt physical robot successfully completing the course.

sections.heading: Conclusion: Real-World Testing Shapes True AI Engineers
sections.summary: RoboBuilder opens new ground for verifying whether AI agents can co-design physical working machines. Simulation is merely a stepping stone; integrating physical tests and video feedback into the loop is essential for practical AI engineering.
sections.details:
This study offers three vital takeaways:

First, the Sim-to-Real gap cannot be bridged without incorporating real-world data. Having the agent calibrate the simulator with real measurements and videos substantially improved physical success, and redesigning from specific failure videos pushed success to 93%. Benchmarks relying solely on simulation scores risk rewarding agents for exploiting physics engine quirks with unrealistic designs.

Second, the core engineering limitation of agents lies not in isolated problem solving, but in system integration. While agents easily cleared individual obstacles, success rates dropped sharply when forced to satisfy conflicting constraints in a single multi-purpose robot. Multi-agent workflows—combining specialized expert agents with an integrating lead agent—are a promising direction forward.

Third, having strong initial engineering concepts matters far more than blindly expanding search budgets. RoboBuilder marks an important first step toward autonomous engineers that take high-level specifications and handle parts selection, mechanical design, control coding, simulation tuning, and physical validation end-to-end.

sections.heading: Appendix: Design Gallery and Agent Thought Processes
sections.summary: The appendix provides a gallery of diverse physical robots that conquered the courses, alongside detailed analytics on how agents conceptualize ideas and iterate over designs.
sections.details:
### A Remarkable Gallery of Physical Robots
The design gallery in the appendix (Figure F8) features surprising mechanisms invented by agents: eccentric cam wheels for climbing stairs, large 3D-printed open-rim hoops for clearing walls, tandem grooved pulley gondolas for gripping ropes, and extended counterweight arms for seesaw balance. These solutions rival human engineering ingenuity.

### Agent Search Style: Sticking to the First Concept
Analyzing agent iteration traces reveals that roughly two-thirds of consecutive simulation steps are local refinements to the same machine. Major structural jumps accounted for only about 4% of steps. Between 50% and 69% of parts in successful designs were already present in the very first simulated design.

Interestingly, exploring a wider variety of conceptual basins did not improve pass rates. The top-performing Opus 5.5 explored the fewest concepts, reaching success by merely fine-tuning its initial concept in 57% of runs. This underscores that an agent's true strength lies not in exhaustive trial-and-error, but in its internal engineering knowledge—enabling it to propose viable concepts right from the start.

captions.F8: Design gallery of robots that crossed the real-world course. Top and middle rows show designs built for individual obstacles (orange parts are custom 3D-printed pieces designed via CAD scripts by agents). The bottom row displays the All-in-one robots developed by each agent to tackle all 10 obstacles with a single machine.

takeaways: LLM agents can autonomously invent creative, functional mechanisms (such as whegs and specialized cams) that conventional search algorithms cannot reach.
Simulation success does not guarantee real-world success, but closing the loop with real run videos boosts physical task completion past 90%.
An agent's design success is driven by the strength of its initial concept rather than search volume, leveraging internalized engineering intuition.
System integration—merging conflicting physical requirements into a single machine—is currently a far bigger hurdle for AI than solving isolated tasks.
limitations: Simulator calibration and failure diagnosis rely on single fixed-camera videos and a few manual measurements, leaving fine-grained contact forces and bending parameters partially unidentified.
Because physical testing required hand-assembling 135 robots, designs received at most 3 physical trials, making it hard to decouple assembly variance and part wear from design flaws.
Current robots are restricted to sensorless, open-loop control (timed velocity commands); co-designing real-time environmental perception and closed-loop feedback remains future work.
